questions.q: The last five closing prices were {a}, {b}, {c}, 104 and 106. What's the 5-day moving average?
questions.why: Add the five closes and divide by 5: {answer}.

questions.q: Why are moving averages, RSI and MACD all called lagging indicators?
options: They're calculated from past prices, so they react after moves happen
They only work on weekly charts
questions.why: They rearrange past prices and volume, so their signals come after the move has started.

questions.q: An RSI above 70 means the price is about to fall.
questions.why: Overbought describes a strong past rise. In strong uptrends RSI can stay above 70 for weeks.

questions.q: Compared with a 10-day moving average, a 200-day moving average is…
options: More jumpy and faster to turn
questions.why: Averaging more days smooths out noise but responds later to changes in trend.

questions.q: A share breaks above resistance on very low volume. What does that suggest?
options: Little conviction: the breakout is easier to reverse
The breakout is certain to continue
questions.why: High volume suggests many participants agree; low volume breakouts fail more easily.

questions.q: Match each indicator to what it measures.
pairs: The average closing price over the last N periods
Recent gains versus recent losses, from 0 to 100
A fast moving average compared with a slow one
How much traded in a period
questions.why: All are summaries of past prices and trading.

questions.q: Trend-following indicators tend to give many false signals when the market moves sideways.
questions.why: In ranges, lines cross back and forth, producing a string of small losing signals called whipsaws.

questions.q: Why doesn't adding six indicators to a chart give six times the information?
options: They're mostly built from the same prices, so they repeat the same information
Charts can only show two indicators
Indicators cancel each other out completely
More indicators always means more profit
questions.why: They mostly rearrange the same price data, so they tend to agree or disagree together.

questions.q: A price starts a new uptrend. Put these in the order they'd usually turn upward.
questions.why: The longer the average, the later it turns: that's the lag.

questions.q: If indicators lag and add no new information, explain how they can still be useful to a trader.

ideas.label: They turn decisions into clear, consistent rules you can follow without emotion
Those rules can be tested on past data, or used as filters to describe conditions

questions.model: They turn a vague feeling into a clear rule you can follow consistently without emotion. And a clear rule can be tested on past data to see whether it has an edge, or used as a filter (for example, only trading with the trend).
questions.why: Indicators help consistency and testing, not prediction.

tests.answer: They give you clear rules to follow without emotion, and you can backtest those rules.

questions.q: A friend sells every share as soon as its RSI goes above 70. Explain the problem with that rule.

ideas.label: In strong uptrends RSI can stay above 70 for a long time while price keeps rising
So they'd miss most of the move: overbought describes the past, not the future

questions.model: In a strong uptrend RSI can stay above 70 for weeks while the price keeps rising, so they'd sell far too early and miss most of the move. Overbought describes how strong the past rise was, not what happens next.
questions.why: An indicator reading isn't a forecast.

tests.answer: In a strong uptrend RSI can stay above 70 for weeks, so they'd sell too soon and miss the move.
